summary:
Mayotte stands under the national framework of France. Identity-document rules, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules governing places of deprivation of liberty apply on the island as French law, and the French prison framework binds Mayotte's establishments as French prisons.

Nothing in that framework criminalises trans people or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been lawful on the island since the 1975 vote to remain within the Republic, and Mayotte is one of few jurisdictions in Africa and in the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document rather than anatomy, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Reporting of 12 January 2018 documents that trans women incarcerated in France are accordingly held in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, and the French prison framework extends to local jails as French establishments.

France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL concluded in an opinion of 25 May 2021 that there is a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. That assessment rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections that interviewed eight trans women and one trans man at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; the establishments it covers include those on Mayotte.

The simplification of legal gender change voted by the French National Assembly is French law and therefore applies on Mayotte, giving trans residents access to the simplified civil-status procedure.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A report of 23 May 2023 describes a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner, pseudonym Abdallah, completing a long and complicated path before marrying at Sada Town Hall, in a predominantly Muslim society where the rights the law confers are not matched by social acceptance.
tangentialFactors:
Mayotte's position is unusual in its wider region: because the island has been part of France since the 1975 vote, same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition are available here, while they are not in most African or Muslim-majority jurisdictions. That rarity raises the weight placed locally on formal French entitlements.

The distance between statutory rights and their exercise is the main turbulence factor. The Sada Town Hall marriage required a prolonged and difficult process despite being lawful, and the reporting frames this as the gap between French rights as written and lived reality on a predominantly Muslim island.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 provides the baseline for expectations inside detention anywhere in France, on the strength of referrals since 2010 covering roughly forty transgender people and of inspections at four establishments. No Mayotte-specific inspection or referral is identified in the sources held here, so conditions on the island are inferred from that national assessment.

Legal-aid infrastructure on the island is thin. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns the message that no lawyer is yet referenced for Mayotte, including for the towns of Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while Maître Isabelle Zribi, a lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation working in persons and family law, is listed as available in Paris.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mayotte marry under the French marriage regime, so same-sex marriage is available at the island's town halls, and trans residents may use the simplified legal gender change voted by the National Assembly as French law.

Residents in trouble with the law are held under the same French prison framework as on the mainland, with placement determined by the identity-document gender marker under Article D248 rather than by anatomy. The national prison conditions assessed by CGLPL, including the serious violations of transgender detainees' rights it identified, apply to the island's establishments as French prisons.

Local legal representation for LGBT residents remains unestablished: the lawyer directory consulted lists no referenced practitioner in Mayotte or its main towns, and points instead to a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation. Anyone needing counsel on the island on a personal-status or family matter would therefore look outside it.

Residents live under the French anti-discrimination statute, but the sources held here record no local complaint, ruling or enforcement action brought under it by a trans person.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports a trans detainee held in Mayotte, a local incident of anti-trans violence, or a local police complaint. Conditions on the island are therefore an extrapolation from French national findings rather than an observed local record.

Whether hormone therapy or other trans-related healthcare is available inside Mayotte's places of deprivation of liberty is unresolved: the sources describe placement rules and rights violations but not medical provision.

The implementing timetable on Mayotte for the simplified legal gender change is not sourced here. The inventory records the National Assembly's vote and its application as French law, without an effective date for civil registries on the island.

No sourced information covers entry screening, visa assessment or the recognition of gender markers on documents issued outside France, nor the treatment of a trans visitor's marital status at the border.

Hate-crime enhancement, its penalties and its enforcement record for offences against trans people in Mayotte are not sourced in this inventory; the anti-discrimination statute is stated to apply as French law, with no local enforcement example available.
